newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Lull in Albania unrest as investors await cash.
newsitem.headline: Lull in Albania unrest as investors await cash.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha said on Wednesday money frozen in failed pyramid scheme savings accounts will be returned to thousands of investors but he could not guarantee they would get all their money back.
Protests have gripped the Balkan state for the past three weeks after get-rich-quick schemes began to crumble, leaving some of Europe's poorest people facing total ruin.
Tempers were calmed after violent clashes at the weekend when the ruling right-wing government vowed to start returning money from February 5. But this may be temporary.
Expressing his regret and solidarity with the people affected by the investment scams, Berisha said the failure of private enterprise was one of the downsides of a free market in a young democracy.
"The date of February 5th fixed by the government will be the starting date for the distribution (of frozen funds)," Berisha told his first news conference since the unrest began.
Asked whether investors will be fully compensated, the president said: "I have never said the people would get all their money back. I have said they would get back the money that has been frozen."

Authorities froze an estimated $300 million deposited by two failed schemes -- Xhaferi and Populli -- in state banks. But the figure was unlikely to be enough to satisfy some people, who sold homes, livestock and possessions to join the investment bandwagon.
Albanian immigrants, many of them working illegally in Italy and neighbouring Greece, sent home their savings to plough into the schemes only to get their fingers burnt.

Some economic analysts believe the pyramid scheme collapse could trigger a fresh wave of immigration from Albania, which may prompt west European states, in particular countries near Albania, into helping to solve the crisis.
Berisha stressed that the government was in no way involved in any of the schemes, nor was it able to bale out investors by printing more money.
"We are determined...to ensure the stability of the currency. There is no greater enemy of the poor than inflation," he said.
He dismissed suggestions that the government had ignored warnings from the International Monetary Fund and Albania's own central bank governor over the pyramid schemes.
The real dangers only became apparent at the end of last year when ministers began taking action, he said.
The finer details of a stable, modern economy may well be lost on many Albanians, especially impoverished rural workers, who feel cheated and just want their money back.

Demonstrators set fire to government buildings and offices of the ruling right-wing Democratic Party in towns in southern Albania, where two failed schemes had been popular. Scores were injured in clashes with riot police in Tirana on Sunday.
Albania's parliament entrusted special powers to Berisha on Sunday, enabling him to use the army to restore order.
Asked how long he would retain the powers, Berisha said: "The period will be short and brief."
Albanian newspapers on Wednesday quoted a statement from the U.S. Pentagon advising Tirana that the army should not violate human rights during the period of unrest.
